slides.say: Nagarjuna's Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way. Chapter five: the examination of the elements.

slides.heading: What is space?
points: Clear a shelf: there is space on it
An invisible container, there all along?
How do we know it is there?
slides.say: Clear a shelf and there is space on it. Take everything out of a room and the room is empty. It seems that space was there all along, a kind of invisible container that things are put into and taken out of, and that would remain if everything were taken away. The fifth chapter asks what this space is, and how we know it is there.

slides.heading: The shape of the chapter
points: Six elements: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind
Space as the hardest case
New tool: a thing and its defining mark
slides.say: The chapter examines the six elements: earth, water, fire, air, space and consciousness. It takes space as its example, because space looked like the hardest case. Some Buddhist schools counted space as unconditioned, existing by its own nature and depending on nothing. If anything had its own nature, space would. The tool of the chapter is new: the relation between a thing and the mark by which it is known, its defining characteristic.

slides.heading: The verses
points: A new translation from the Sanskrit
Eight verses
slides.say: First, the verses. The translation is new, made from the Sanskrit for this site.

slides.heading: A thing and its mark
points: Fire by heat, water by wetness, earth by solidity
Space is known by not obstructing
How is the mark related to the space?
slides.say: Now the explanation. How do we know what anything is? By its marks. Fire is known by heat, water by wetness, earth by solidity. The Abhidharma called this a thing's defining characteristic: the mark that makes it what it is and sets it apart from everything else. The defining characteristic of space is that it does not obstruct. Space is what makes room. Where there is a wall, you cannot put your hand; where there is space, you can. The chapter asks how this mark is related to the space that has it.

slides.heading: Space before its mark?
slides.say: Is there space first, which then has the mark of making room? If so, before the mark arrived, the space would have had no mark at all. It would be a thing with no characteristic. But no such thing is ever found. Space that does not make room, does not give way, does nothing to show itself, is not space. It is not anything we could point to or name.

slides.heading: Where does the mark land?
slides.say: Turn it around. Where does the characteristic apply? Not to something that has no characteristic, because there is no such thing. Not to something that already has its characteristic, because then the mark would have nothing to add; it would be applying itself twice. And there is no third kind of thing, neither with a mark nor without one, for the mark to land on. The mark and what it marks cannot meet as two separate things.

slides.heading: Designated together
slides.say: So, as verses four and five say, if the mark does not apply, there is nothing marked. If there is nothing marked, there is nothing for the mark to be a mark of. Characteristic and characterised stand or fall together. Neither is found on its own, and no thing is found apart from both. This is the same shape as condition and effect in chapter one, walker and walking in chapter two, and form and its cause in chapter four. Here it reaches the very way we identify anything at all. And room is always room for something. The container that would remain if everything were removed is assumed, not found.

slides.heading: Not even an absence
points: An absence is always an absence of something
Who stands outside presence and absence?
The other elements go the same way
slides.say: Here the opponent might say: very well, space is not a thing. Then it is simply nothing, an absence. Nagarjuna closes that door too. An absence is always the absence of something. No milk in the fridge is an absence of milk. If there is no self-standing thing, there is no self-standing absence of it either. And who, standing outside both presence and absence, would know them? To call space a thing or a nothing, one would need a viewpoint outside both, and no such viewpoint is found. So space is not a thing, not an absence, not something marked and not a mark. Earth, water, fire, air and consciousness are just like it.

slides.heading: Neither existence nor non-existence
points: 'It exists': the extreme of permanence
'It does not exist': the extreme of annihilation
Both fall away: a quieting, not a blank
slides.say: The chapter ends with a verse that sets the tone for the rest of the work. Those of little understanding see things as existing or as not existing. They miss the peaceful quieting of what is to be seen. Seeing things as existing, with their own nature, is the extreme of permanence. Seeing them as nothing at all is the extreme of annihilation. Both picture something with a definite status. When the thing with whereabouts is not found, both views fall away together, and what is left is called quieting. It is not a blank. The room is still there to walk into. Only the frantic sorting of everything into is and is not quiets down.

slides.heading: What is left standing
points: You can still put a vase on the shelf
Space as room for something
Real as what it does, and nothing more
slides.say: You can still clear a shelf and put a vase on it. Architects still design rooms, and physicists still measure distances. The chapter takes away only the picture of space as a self-standing container, existing before and apart from anything that could occupy it. What remains is space as it is actually met: room for something, distance between things, the give that lets a hand pass. Space is real as what it does, and nothing more is needed.

slides.heading: Check it now
points: Look at the space in front of you
Look for it apart from the room it gives
Openness, and no container behind it
slides.say: Look at the empty space in front of you. Look for space apart from the room it gives, apart from the distance to the wall, apart from the openness your hand could move through. What do you find? Openness, vivid and usable, and no container behind it.

slides.heading: In the books
points: Substrateless World: Interlude and Chapter 13
The Logic of Dependency (bonus article)
Anatta to Emptiness: Space Is Also a Formation
slides.say: The two books take up these themes in several places. In The Logical Necessity of a Substrateless World, the Interlude, on space, and chapter thirteen, on the mark and the marked. The bonus article, The Logic of Dependency, on space pictured as a container. And in The Transition from Anatta to Emptiness, the chapter Space Is Also a Formation. Links to all of them are on the chapter page. Next: chapter six, the examination of desire and the desirous.
